column2: And they came to hollow, wide-ravined Lacedaemon,
and drove to the house of glorious Menelaus.
Him they found giving a wedding feast, for many of his kin,
for his blameless son and daughter in his house.
The daughter he was sending to the son of Achilles, breaker of men;
for in Troy he had first promised and nodded assent
to give her, and now the gods were bringing the marriage to pass for them.
Her then he was sending with horses and chariots to go
to the far-famed city of the Myrmidons, over whom he ruled.
And for his son he was bringing from Sparta the daughter of Alector,
who had been born to him, strong Megapenthes, a late-born child
of a slave woman; for to Helen the gods showed no further offspring,
after she had borne at first a lovely child,
Hermione, who had the form of golden Aphrodite.
So they feasted throughout the great high-roofed house,
the neighbours and kinsmen of glorious Menelaus,
enjoying themselves; and among them a divine singer sang
playing the lyre, and two tumblers among them,
as the singer began the song, whirled in the midst.
And these two, at the forecourt of the house, themselves and their horses,
the hero Telemachus and the glorious son of Nestor,
stopped; and coming forth lord Eteoneus saw them,
the busy attendant of glorious Menelaus,
and he went to bring word through the house to the shepherd of the people,
and standing near him addressed him with winged words:

Two strangers here, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus,
27	two men, and in lineage like great Zeus.
28	But tell me, shall we unyoke the swift horses for them,
29	or send them on to another to receive them, who will welcome them?
And greatly vexed, fair-haired Menelaus said to him:

You were not foolish, Eteoneus, son of Boethous,
32	before; but now you speak like a child, foolish things.
33	Surely we two came here, having eaten much hospitality
34	of other men, in case Zeus
35	may afterwards end our misery. But unyoke the horses
36	of the strangers, and lead them in to be feasted.
So he spoke, and the other rushed through the hall, and called the other
busy attendants to follow along with himself.
And they loosed the sweating horses from the yoke,
and tied them at the horses' mangers,
and threw beside them spelt, and mixed in white barley,
and leaned the chariots against the shining walls,
and led the men into the divine house. And they, seeing it,
marvelled at the house of the Zeus-nurtured king;
for there was a gleam as of the sun or the moon
through the high-roofed house of glorious Menelaus.
But when they had taken their fill of looking with their eyes,
they went to the well-polished baths and bathed.
And when the maids had bathed them and anointed them with oil,
and cast about them woollen cloaks and tunics,
they sat on chairs beside Menelaus, son of Atreus.
A handmaid brought water in a fair golden pitcher
and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash; and she drew up beside them a polished table.
And the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by,
adding many dishes, giving of what she had in store.
And a carver lifted and set by platters of meats
of all kinds, and set beside them golden cups.
Greeting the two, fair-haired Menelaus said:

Take of the food and rejoice. And afterwards,
61	when you have had your fill of supper, we shall ask who you are
62	among men; for the lineage of your parents has not perished in you,
63	but you are of a line of men, Zeus-nurtured kings,
64	sceptre-bearers, since base men could not beget such as you.
So he spoke, and took in his hands and set before them
the rich back of an ox, roasted, which they had set before him as his honour.
And they stretched out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
But when they had put away the desire for drink and food,
then Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor,
holding his head close, that the others might not hear:

Consider, son of Nestor, delight of my heart,
72	the flash of bronze through the echoing halls,
73	and of gold and amber and silver and ivory.
74	Such, I think, is the court of Olympian Zeus within,
75	so many unspeakable things are here; awe holds me as I look.
Fair-haired Menelaus heard him as he spoke,
and speaking to them addressed them with winged words:

Dear children, with Zeus no mortal could contend;
79	for his houses and possessions are immortal;
80	but of men, one may or may not contend with me
81	in possessions. For having suffered much and wandered much
82	I brought them in my ships and came in the eighth year,
83	having wandered to Cyprus and Phoenicia and the Egyptians,
84	and I came to the Ethiopians and Sidonians and Erembi
85	and Libya, where lambs are at once horned.
86	For three times the flocks bear in a full year.
87	There neither master nor shepherd is in want
88	of cheese or meat or sweet milk,
89	but always they provide milk to be drawn all the year.
90	While I wandered about those places gathering much livelihood,
91	meanwhile another man killed my brother
92	secretly, unlooked for, by the guile of his accursed wife;
93	so I do not rule over these possessions with joy.
94	And of your fathers you must be hearing this, whoever they are
95	to you, since I suffered very much, and lost a house
96	well inhabited, holding many fine things.
97	Of these I wish I lived in my house with a third part,
98	and that those men were safe, who then perished
99	in wide Troy, far from horse-nurturing Argos.
100	But yet, lamenting and grieving for them all,
101	often sitting in our halls,
102	at one time I take pleasure in my heart in lament, and at another
103	I cease; quickly comes satiety of chilling lament.
104	Of them all I do not so much mourn, grieved though I am,
105	as for one, who makes sleep and food hateful to me
106	when I remember, since no Achaean toiled so much
107	as Odysseus toiled and endured. And for him it was to be
108	sorrow for himself, and for me an unforgettable grief always
109	for him, how long he has been gone, and we know nothing,
110	whether he lives or is dead. Perhaps they mourn him,
111	old Laertes and prudent Penelope
112	and Telemachus, whom he left a newborn in the house.
So he spoke, and in him raised a longing to weep for his father.
He let a tear fall to the ground from his eyelids, hearing of his father,
holding up his purple cloak before his eyes
with both hands. And Menelaus noticed him,
and then he pondered in his mind and in his heart,
whether to let him himself mention his father
or first to question him and try out each thing.
While he was pondering these things in his mind and in his heart,
Helen came out of her fragrant high-roofed chamber,
like Artemis of the golden distaff.
With her Adreste placed a well-made chair,
and Alcippe brought a rug of soft wool,
and Phylo brought a silver basket, which Alcandre
gave her, wife of Polybus, who lived in Egyptian Thebes,
where most possessions lie in the houses;
he gave Menelaus two silver baths,
two tripods, and ten talents of gold.
And separately his wife gave Helen beautiful gifts:
she gave a golden distaff and a wheeled basket
of silver, and its rims were finished with gold.
This the handmaid Phylo brought and set beside her,
filled with spun yarn; and on it
the distaff was stretched, holding violet-dark wool.
She sat on a chair, and a footstool was beneath her feet.
At once she questioned her husband with words on each point:

Do we know, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, who these men
139	claim to be, who have come to our house?
140	Shall I lie or speak the truth? My heart bids me.
141	For I say I have never yet seen anyone so like,
142	neither man nor woman, awe holds me as I look,
143	as this man is like the son of great-hearted Odysseus,
144	Telemachus, whom that man left a newborn in the house,
145	when for the sake of me, shameless, the Achaeans
146	came beneath Troy, pondering bold war.
Answering her, fair-haired Menelaus said:

So now I too think, woman, as you suppose;
149	for his feet were such, and such his hands,
150	the glances of his eyes, and his head and the hair above.
151	And now indeed, remembering Odysseus,
152	I was telling how much he toiled and suffered
153	for my sake, and he shed a bitter tear beneath his brows,
154	holding up his purple cloak before his eyes.
Then Nestor's son Peisistratus answered him in turn:

Son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, leader of the people,
157	this is truly that man's son, as you say;
158	but he is prudent, and feels shame in his heart
159	to come thus at first and show forward words
160	before you, in whose voice we delight as in a god's.
161	But Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, sent me
162	to follow with him as escort; for he wished to see you,
163	so that you might suggest to him some word or some deed.
164	For a son has many pains when his father is gone
165	in the halls, if he has no other helpers,
166	as now Telemachus' father is gone, and he has no others
167	who could ward off evil in the district.
Answering him, fair-haired Menelaus said:

Oh dear, truly the son of a dear man has come
170	to my house, who for my sake endured many labours;
171	and I thought that when he came I would love him above the other
172	Argives, if over the sea Olympian, wide-seeing Zeus
173	had given us two a return in our swift ships.
174	And I would have settled him in Argos and built him a city and a house,
175	bringing him from Ithaca with his possessions and his child
176	and all his people, having emptied one city,
177	of those that dwell around, and are ruled by me myself.
178	And often, being here, we would have mingled; and nothing else
179	would have parted us, loving and rejoicing,
180	before the dark cloud of death enfolded us.
181	But these things the god himself must have begrudged,
182	who made that unhappy man alone without return.
So he spoke, and in them all he raised a longing to weep.
Argive Helen wept, born of Zeus,
and Telemachus wept, and Menelaus son of Atreus,
nor did the son of Nestor keep his eyes tearless;
for he remembered in his heart blameless Antilochus,
whom the glorious son of bright Dawn had killed;
remembering him he spoke winged words:

Son of Atreus, you are wise beyond mortals,
191	old Nestor used to say, when we spoke of you
192	in his halls, and asked one another.
193	And now, if it is at all possible, obey me; for I
194	take no pleasure in lamenting after supper, but also dawn
195	will be early-born; yet I feel no shame at all
196	to weep for whichever mortal dies and meets his fate.
197	This is the only honour for wretched mortals,
198	to cut the hair and let fall a tear from the cheeks.
199	For my brother too has died, by no means the worst
200	of the Argives; and you must know him; for I
201	did not meet or see him; but they say that beyond others
202	Antilochus was, exceedingly swift of foot and a fighter.
Answering him, fair-haired Menelaus said:

My friend, since you have said as much as a wise man
205	would say and do, even one who is older;
206	for you are of such a father, so you speak wisely,
207	and easily recognized is the offspring of a man for whom the son of Cronos
208	spins happiness at his marriage and at his birth,
209	as now he has given Nestor continually all his days
210	himself to grow old in prosperity in his halls,
211	and his sons to be wise and best with the spear.
212	But we shall leave the weeping that was before,
213	and let us again think of supper, and let them pour water
214	on our hands. And there will be talk also in the morning
215	for Telemachus and me to tell one another.
So he spoke, and Asphalion poured water on their hands,
the busy attendant of glorious Menelaus.
And they stretched out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
Then Helen, born of Zeus, thought of another thing.
At once she cast into the wine they were drinking a drug,
a care-banishing, anger-quelling one, bringing forgetfulness of all evils.
Whoever drank it down, when it was mixed in the bowl,
would not for that day let fall a tear down his cheeks,
not even if his mother and father lay dead,
not even if before him his brother or dear son
were slain with bronze, and he saw it with his own eyes.
Such cunning drugs the daughter of Zeus had,
good ones, which Polydamna gave her, the wife of Thon,
an Egyptian, where the grain-giving earth bears most
drugs, many good when mixed, and many baneful.
and every man a physician, knowing beyond all
men; for they are of the race of Paieon.
But when she had put it in and bidden them pour the wine,
again she answered with words and spoke:

Son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, and you also,
236	children of good men; but god Zeus gives now to one, now to another,
237	good and evil; for he can do all things.
238	Now indeed feast sitting in the halls
239	and take pleasure in tales; for I shall tell fitting ones.
240	All of them I could not tell or name,
241	as many as are the labours of much-enduring Odysseus;
242	but of what sort was this that the mighty man did and endured
243	in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes.
244	Having subdued himself with unseemly blows,
245	throwing a wretched rag about his shoulders, like a servant,
246	he entered the wide-wayed city of hostile men;
247	and hiding himself he made himself like another man,
248	a beggar, who was in no way such at the ships of the Achaeans.
249	Like him he entered the city of the Trojans, and they were all
250	blind to it; but I alone recognized him, being such,
251	and I questioned him; but he with cunning avoided me.
252	But when I had washed him and anointed him with oil,
253	and put clothes about him, and swore a mighty oath
254	not to reveal Odysseus among the Trojans
255	before he had come to the swift ships and the huts,
256	then he told me all the plan of the Achaeans.
257	And having killed many of the Trojans with the long-edged bronze
258	he went to the Argives, and brought back much knowledge.
259	Then the other Trojan women wailed loudly; but my heart
260	rejoiced, since already my heart had turned to go
261	home again, and I lamented the folly which Aphrodite
262	gave, when she led me there from my dear native land,
263	having forsaken my child and my bridal chamber and my husband,
264	who lacked nothing, neither in mind nor in looks.
Answering her, fair-haired Menelaus said:

Yes indeed, woman, all this you have said according to what is right.
267	Already I have learned the counsel and mind of many
268	heroes, and I have gone over much land;
269	but never yet have I seen with my eyes any such
270	as the heart of much-enduring Odysseus was.
271	Such a thing too the mighty man did and endured
272	in the polished horse, where all of us, the best
273	of the Argives, sat, bringing slaughter and doom to the Trojans.
274	Then you came there; and a deity must have bidden you,
275	who wished to grant glory to the Trojans;
276	and godlike Deiphobus followed you as you went.
277	Three times you went round the hollow ambush, feeling it,
278	and you called by name the best of the Danaans,
279	making your voice like the wives of all the Argives.
280	But I and the son of Tydeus and godlike Odysseus
281	sat in the midst and heard how you called out.
282	Both of us two were eager and set out
283	either to go out, or to answer at once from within;
284	but Odysseus held us back and restrained us, eager though we were.
285	Then all the other sons of the Achaeans were silent,
286	and Anticlus alone wished to answer you
287	with words. But Odysseus pressed his jaw with his hands
288	steadily, mighty ones, and saved all the Achaeans;
289	and so he held, until Pallas Athena led you away.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

Son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, leader of the people,
292	the more grievous; for these things did not ward off grievous death for him,
293	not even if his heart within had been of iron.
294	But come, turn us to bed, that even now
295	we may be satisfied, lying down to sweet sleep.
So he spoke, and Argive Helen ordered the maids
to place beds under the portico and to throw on fair
purple blankets and to spread rugs over them,
and to put woollen cloaks on top to be covered with.
And they went out of the hall holding torches in their hands,
and spread the beds; and a herald led the guests out.
So they slept there in the forecourt of the house,
the hero Telemachus and the glorious son of Nestor;
and the son of Atreus slept in the inner part of the lofty house,
and beside him lay Helen of the long robe, bright among women.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
Menelaus, good at the war-cry, rose from his bed,
put on his clothes, and slung a sharp sword about his shoulder,
and under his shining feet bound fair sandals,
and went to go out from his chamber, like a god to look upon.
and sat beside Telemachus, and spoke a word and called him by name:

What need has brought you here, hero Telemachus,
313	to divine Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
314	Public or private? Tell me this truly.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

Son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, leader of the people,
317	I have come in case you can tell me some report of my father.
318	My house is being eaten, and the rich works are ruined,
319	and my house is full of hostile men, who always
320	slaughter my crowded sheep and my shambling, crook-horned cattle,
321	the suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence.
322	Therefore now I come to your knees, if you are willing
323	to tell of his grievous death, if somewhere you saw it
324	with your own eyes or heard the tale from another
325	wanderer; for his mother bore him beyond others to suffer.
326	And do not soften anything out of respect for me or pity,
327	but tell me well how you came to see it.
328	I beseech you, if ever my father, good Odysseus,
329	undertook and fulfilled for you any word or deed
330	in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes,
331	remember these things now for me, and tell me truly.
And greatly vexed, fair-haired Menelaus said to him:

Oh dear, truly in the bed of a man stout of heart
334	they wished to lie, being themselves without valour.
335	As when in a thicket a hind has laid down her newborn
336	suckling fawns of a mighty lion
337	and ranges over the hill-slopes and grassy glens
338	grazing, and then he comes into his own lair,
339	and sends an unseemly fate upon both of them,
340	so Odysseus will send an unseemly fate upon those men.
341	Would that, father Zeus and Athena and Apollo,
342	being such as once in well-built Lesbos
343	he rose up in a quarrel and wrestled with Philomeleides,
344	and threw him down mightily, and all the Achaeans rejoiced,
345	being such Odysseus might meet the suitors;
346	all would be short-lived and bitter in their marrying.
347	But what you ask me and beseech, I would not
348	speak otherwise, turning aside, nor will I deceive you,
349	but what the old man of the sea, who speaks unerringly, told me,
350	of that I will hide no word from you nor conceal it.
351	In Egypt the gods held me, still eager to come
352	back here, since I had not offered them perfect hecatombs.
353	And the gods always wished us to remember their commands.
354	Then there is an island in the much-washed sea
355	in front of Egypt, and they call it Pharos,
356	as far away as a hollow ship goes in a whole day
357	when a shrill wind blows behind it;
358	and on it is a harbour with good anchorage, whence they
359	launch the balanced ships into the sea, having drawn dark water.
360	There the gods held me twenty days, and never did the winds
361	blowing over the sea appear, which are
362	the escorts of ships over the broad back of the sea.
363	And now all provisions would have been used up, and the strength of the men,
364	had not one of the gods pitied me and saved me,
365	Eidothea, daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea;
366	for her above all I had stirred the heart.
367	She met me as I wandered alone, apart from my companions;
368	for they were always wandering round the island fishing
369	with bent hooks, and hunger wore at their belly.
370	She stood near me and spoke a word and said:
371	'You are very foolish, stranger, and slack of mind,
372	or do you willingly give way and take pleasure in suffering pains?
373	For you are held so long on the island, and can find no end,
374	and the heart of your companions is wasting away.'
375	So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
376	'I will tell you, whoever you are of the goddesses,
377	that I am not held here willingly, but I must have
378	sinned against the immortals, who hold the broad heaven.
379	But you tell me, for the gods know all things,
380	which of the immortals binds me and has fettered me from my path,
381	and my return, how I shall go over the fishy sea.'
382	So I spoke, and at once the bright one among goddesses answered:
383	'Therefore, stranger, I shall tell you very exactly.
384	There frequents this place an old man of the sea who speaks unerringly,
385	immortal Egyptian Proteus, who knows the depths
386	of all the sea, a servant of Poseidon;
387	and they say that he is my father and begot me.
388	If somehow you could lie in ambush and seize him,
389	he would tell you the way and the measures of the journey
390	and your return, how you will go over the fishy sea.
391	And he will tell you, Zeus-nurtured one, if you wish,
392	what evil and good have come to pass in your halls
393	since you went on your long and painful journey.'
394	So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
395	'You yourself now devise the ambush for the godlike old man,
396	lest somehow seeing me beforehand or knowing beforehand he avoid me;
397	for a god is hard for a mortal man to subdue.'
398	So I spoke, and at once the bright one among goddesses answered:
399	'Therefore, stranger, I shall tell you very exactly.
400	When the sun has taken his stand in the middle of heaven,
401	then the old man of the sea who speaks unerringly comes out of the sea,
402	under the breath of Zephyr, covered by a dark ripple,
403	and coming out he sleeps beneath the hollow caves;
404	and around him the seals, the offspring of fair Halosydne,
405	sleep in a crowd, having come up out of the grey sea,
406	breathing out the bitter smell of the deep sea.
407	There I shall lead you at the appearing of dawn
408	and lay you in a row; and you choose well three companions,
409	those who are the best by your well-benched ships.
410	And I shall tell you all the baneful tricks of that old man.
411	First he will count the seals and go over them;
412	but when he has counted them all by fives and seen them,
413	he will lie down in the middle, like a shepherd among flocks of sheep.
414	As soon as you see him laid to sleep,
415	then let your strength and might be your care,
416	and hold him there, though eager and rushing to escape.
417	And becoming everything he will try you, all that on the earth
418	creeps, and water, and blazing fire;
419	but you hold him fast and press the more.
420	But when he himself questions you in words,
421	being such as you saw him when he was laid to sleep,
422	then cease from force and loose the old man,
423	hero, and ask which of the gods is angry with you,
424	and your return, how you will go over the fishy sea.'
425	So saying she plunged beneath the surging sea.
426	And I went to the ships, where they stood on the sand,
427	and my heart was much stirred as I went.
428	But when I had come down to the ship and the sea,
429	and we had made ready supper, and ambrosial night came on,
430	then we lay down on the shore of the sea.
431	When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
432	then I went along the shore of the broad-wayed sea,
433	praying much to the gods; and I took three companions,
434	in whom I trusted most for every venture.
435	Meanwhile she, having plunged into the broad bosom of the sea,
436	brought four seal-skins from the deep;
437	and all were freshly flayed; and she devised a trick for her father.
438	Having scooped out beds in the sandy shore
439	she sat waiting; and we came very close to her;
440	in order she laid us down, and threw a skin over each.
441	There the ambush would have been most dreadful; for terribly distressed us
442	the most deadly smell of the sea-nurtured seals;
443	for who would lie down beside a sea-monster?
444	But she herself saved us and devised a great boon;
445	she brought ambrosia and put it under each one's nose,
446	breathing very sweetly, and destroyed the smell of the monster.
447	All the morning we waited with enduring heart;
448	and the seals came out of the sea in a crowd. Then they
449	lay down in a row along the shore of the sea;
450	and at noon the old man came out of the sea, and found the seals
451	well fed, and went over them all, and counted their number;
452	and among the monsters he counted us first, and in his mind
453	did not suspect that there was a trick; then he lay down himself.
454	And we rushed on with a shout, and threw our hands
455	about him; nor did the old man forget his crafty art,
456	but first he became a bearded lion,
457	and then a serpent and a leopard and a great boar;
458	and he became flowing water and a tall-leaved tree;
459	but we held fast with enduring heart.
460	But when the old man, who knew baneful tricks, grew weary,
461	then at last he spoke to me and questioned me with words:
462	'Which of the gods, son of Atreus, took counsel with you,
463	that you should seize me against my will, lying in ambush? What do you need?'
464	So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
465	'You know, old man, why do you ask me this, turning aside?
466	How long I am held on the island, and can find no end,
467	and my heart wastes away within me.
468	But you tell me, for the gods know all things,
469	which of the immortals binds me and has fettered me from my path,
470	and my return, how I shall go over the fishy sea.'
471	So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:
472	'But you ought, to Zeus and the other gods,
473	having offered fair sacrifices, to embark, that as quickly as possible
474	you may reach your native land, sailing over the wine-dark sea.
475	For it is not your fate to see your friends and to reach
476	your well-built house and your native land,
477	before you go again to the water of Egypt, the Zeus-fallen river,
478	and offer sacred hecatombs
479	to the immortal gods, who hold the broad heaven;
480	and then the gods will give you the way you desire.'
481	So he spoke, and my dear heart was broken,
482	because he bade me go again over the misty sea
483	to Egypt, a long and painful way.
484	But even so I answered with words and said:
485	'These things I shall accomplish thus, old man, as you bid.
486	But come, tell me this, and relate it exactly:
487	whether all the Achaeans came unharmed with their ships,
488	whom Nestor and I left coming from Troy,
489	or whether any perished by a death of misery on his own ship
490	or in the hands of friends, after he had wound up the war.'
491	So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:
492	'Son of Atreus, why do you ask me this? There is no need for you
493	to know, nor to learn my mind; and I say that you
494	will not be long without tears, when you have learned it all well.
495	For many of them were subdued, and many were left;
496	and only two leaders of the bronze-coated Achaeans
497	perished on the return; and in the battle you were present too.
498	And one still lives somewhere, held back on the broad sea.
499	Ajax was subdued among his long-oared ships.
500	First Poseidon brought him near the Gyrae,
